name: Movement of substances in and out of cells

questions.q: What is the biological definition of diffusion?
a: The net movement of particles from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement
The movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane
The active uptake of ions requiring cellular energy (ATP)
The bulk flow of blood through vessels driven by heart contractions

questions.q: Which of the following factors increases the rate of diffusion?
a: A lower temperature
A steeper concentration gradient and a higher temperature
A thicker diffusion distance
A smaller surface area-to-volume ratio

questions.q: What is osmosis defined as?
a: The movement of solute particles from low to high concentration
The active transport of mineral salts across root hair membranes
The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane
The evaporation of water from leaf stomata

questions.q: What happens to a plant cell when placed in a pure water solution (high water potential)?
a: It shrinks and becomes plasmolysed
It undergoes lysis and bursts
It remains completely unchanged
Water enters by osmosis, causing the vacuole to swell and the cell to become turgid

questions.q: What term describes a plant cell that has lost water by osmosis, causing the cell membrane to pull away from the cell wall?
a: Plasmolysed
Turgid
Flaccid
Crenated

questions.q: What happens to a red blood cell when placed in a concentrated salt solution (very low water potential)?
a: It swells and bursts (lysis)
It loses water by osmosis, shrinks, and becomes crenated (shrivelled)
It becomes turgid and rigid
It divides by mitosis

questions.q: What is active transport defined as?
a: The passive movement of molecules down a concentration gradient
The random thermal motion of particles in a gas or liquid
The movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration using energy from respiration
The mass flow of water through xylem vessels

questions.q: Why is cellular respiration essential for active transport to take place?
a: Because respiration produces water molecules
Because respiration lowers the temperature of the cell
Because respiration produces carbon dioxide gas
Because active transport requires ATP energy released during respiration to drive carrier proteins

questions.q: Which of the following substances moves into plant root hair cells via active transport when their concentration in the soil is lower than inside the cell?
a: Nitrate and other mineral ions
Oxygen gas molecules
Water molecules
Carbon dioxide gas

questions.q: How does surface area-to-volume ratio affect the rate of movement of substances into and out of single-celled versus large multicellular organisms?
a: Larger organisms have a higher surface area-to-volume ratio, making diffusion very fast
Smaller organisms have a large surface area-to-volume ratio, allowing efficient diffusion across their cell surface, whereas large organisms require specialized transport systems
Surface area has no impact on transport rates
Volume decreases diffusion rates in bacteria

questions.q: Which of the following is a classic example of diffusion occurring in the human gas exchange system?
a: Glucose moving from the gut into villi capillaries
Water reabsorption in kidney tubules
Oxygen diffusing from alveoli into lung capillaries, and carbon dioxide diffusing in the reverse direction
Mineral ions moving into root hairs

questions.q: What role do protein carrier molecules play in the cell membrane?
a: They provide structural support like a rigid cell wall
They synthesize lipids for the cell
They store genetic information
They bind to specific molecules and change shape to transport them across the membrane during active transport or facilitated diffusion

questions.q: Which of the following describes a flaccid plant cell?
a: A cell that has lost some water, making the tissues limp because turgor pressure has decreased
A cell that has burst due to excess water intake
A cell packed tightly with rigid sucrose crystals
A dead cell with no membrane

questions.q: Why do animal cells burst when placed in pure water, whereas plant cells do not?
a: Animal cells lack cytoplasm
Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall to resist the inward pressure of entering water, whereas plant cells have a strong cellulose wall
Plant cells actively pump water out using energy
Animal cells have waterproof membranes

questions.q: What property of a cell membrane makes it selective about which molecules can pass through freely via simple diffusion?
a: It is completely impermeable to all substances
It is an active muscular pump
It is partially (selectively) permeable, allowing small molecules like oxygen and water to pass while blocking large molecules like starch
It is made of thick wood

questions.q: How does temperature influence the rate of diffusion?
a: Higher temperatures slow down particle movement
Temperature has no effect on kinetic energy
Higher temperatures decrease molecular collisions
Higher temperatures increase the kinetic energy of particles, causing them to move faster and increasing the rate of diffusion

questions.q: Which of the following gases diffuses out of a green plant leaf during daylight hours?
a: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Water vapor exclusively

questions.q: What is the term for water movement across a partially permeable membrane driven by differences in water potential?
a: Active transport
Osmosis
Diffusion
Transpiration

questions.q: If a plant's roots are poisoned by a chemical that stops cellular respiration, what will happen to the uptake of mineral ions?
a: Ion uptake will increase rapidly
Ion uptake will remain completely unaffected
Ion uptake will stop because active transport requires ATP from respiration
Ions will diffuse out of the roots

questions.q: How does the concentration gradient affect the rate of diffusion?
a: A steeper concentration gradient slows down net movement
Concentration gradients only affect active transport
A concentration gradient has no impact on particle speed
A steeper concentration gradient (a larger difference in concentration between two regions) results in a faster rate of diffusion

questions.q: Which of the following represents diffusion of water specifically?
a: Osmosis
Active transport
Translocation
Peristalsis

questions.q: What happens to glucose absorption in the human small intestine when the concentration of glucose in the gut lumen becomes lower than inside the blood?
a: Diffusion stops entirely
Glucose is absorbed via active transport using carrier proteins and energy
Glucose moves out of the blood into the gut
Osmosis reverses direction

questions.q: Why do multicellular organisms need specialized exchange surfaces (like alveoli or villi)?
a: Because they are exposed to sunlight
Because their cells do not need oxygen
Because their low surface area-to-volume ratio means simple diffusion across their outer skin is too slow to supply inner cells
Because they lack cell membranes

questions.q: What happens to plant tissues (such as potato strips) when placed in a concentrated sucrose solution?
a: They absorb water, swell, and become hard
They produce starch granules
They undergo cell division
They lose water by osmosis, decrease in mass, and become soft/flaccid

questions.q: Which of the following molecules is small enough to diffuse freely through the lipid bilayer of a cell membrane?
a: Oxygen and carbon dioxide
Starch molecules
Protein molecules
Glycogen granules

questions.q: What term describes the condition of a red blood cell placed in pure water?
a: Crenation
Lysis (bursting)
Plasmolysis
Flaccidity

questions.q: How does diffusion distance affect the rate at which substances reach the center of a cell or tissue?
a: Thicker diffusion distances speed up transport
Diffusion distance does not matter
A shorter diffusion distance speeds up diffusion, whereas a longer distance slows it down significantly
Longer distances stop all molecular motion

questions.q: What is the primary source of energy that drives simple diffusion?
a: ATP produced by mitochondria
Sunlight absorbed by pigments
Chemical energy from food digestion
The intrinsic kinetic energy (random thermal motion) of the particles themselves

questions.q: Which biological process moves mineral ions into plant roots against a concentration gradient?
a: Active transport
Osmosis
Simple diffusion
Transpiration pull

questions.q: Why is turgor pressure important for non-woody (herbaceous) plants?
a: It provides the energy required for photosynthesis
It supports stems and leaves, keeping them upright and exposing maximum surface area to sunlight
It prevents water from evaporating
It drives active transport in roots

questions.q: What is water potential?
a: A measure of the physical pressure inside a blood vessel
The speed at which water molecules evaporate from leaves
A measure of the tendency of water molecules to move from one place to another (higher in pure water)
The chemical energy stored in hydrogen bonds

questions.q: Which of the following cellular structures acts as the boundary that facilitates selective transport?
a: Cellulose cell wall
Cytoplasm
Nucleus
Cell membrane

questions.q: What causes plant cells to become plasmolysed when placed in concentrated syrup?
a: Water moves out of the cell down a water potential gradient by osmosis
Sugar molecules actively pump water out
Cell walls dissolve in syrup
Cells absorb too much sugar and burst

questions.q: Which of the following describes how gas exchange occurs in single-celled organisms like amoeba?
a: Through specialized lungs
Via simple diffusion directly across the cell membrane due to a high surface area-to-volume ratio
Through active transport requiring ATP
Via xylem vessels

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing the surface area of an exchange surface (such as villi folds in the small intestine)?
a: It decreases the absorption rate
It has no effect on transport
It increases the rate of diffusion and active transport of nutrients
It stops osmosis completely

questions.q: Why can large protein molecules not pass through a partially permeable cell membrane during dialysis tubing experiments?
a: Because they are gaseous
Because they dissolve in water
Because they carry an electrical charge
Because their molecular size is too large to fit through the microscopic pores in the membrane

questions.q: What happens to the rate of active transport if a metabolic poison is added that blocks cellular respiration?
a: Active transport stops because ATP production ceases
Active transport speeds up
Diffusion stops instead
Osmosis increases

questions.q: Which of the following processes is entirely passive and does not require cellular energy (ATP)?
a: Active transport
Diffusion and osmosis
Endocytosis
Protein synthesis

questions.q: How does the permeability of a cell membrane affect substance movement?
a: It blocks all water molecules completely
It allows any sized molecule to enter freely
It selectively allows certain small molecules to pass while restricting others, maintaining internal cellular conditions
It actively digests foreign particles
